items.title: Explainer: Five ways US foreign policy may change with a Democratic Congress
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 4 - Democrats secured control of the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterm elections, giving them an important slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.

During the campaign, Democrats had argued that Republicans ceded Congress's constitutional war-making and spending powers to the administration of President Donald Trump. They are now expected to curb those powers.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy.

CURB THE IRAN WAR

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran alongside Israel on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he seeks congressional authorization. One of these resolutions passed both the House and Senate with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump's administration ignored it.

With their new influence, Democrats could cut defense spending or hold up nominations to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to keep lawmakers and the public informed, including at public hearings, about their plans.

FRESH SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE

Trump has largely halted direct financial and military aid to Ukraine, which is fighting a Russian invasion, despite broad support for the US assistance from Democratic and Republican lawmakers.

Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy, weeks after signing them into law.

With control of both chambers starting in January, Democrats will be able to decide what gets voted on and when. That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto. Democratic aides have said assisting Kyiv is a priority.

They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Democratic Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who is likely to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump's plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.

While the final size of the Democratic majorities has not been determined, backing for Ukraine has been so strong in the past from both that party and many of Trump's Republicans that Congress may be able to muster majorities large enough to override a Trump veto.

END MILITARY AID TO ISRAEL

Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.

Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which includes a base $3.8 billion per year, plus billions of dollars more since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that led to the devastating Israeli campaign in Gaza.

Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.

LIMIT MILITARY SPENDING AND RESTORE FOREIGN AID

Democrats are far more likely than Trump's Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.

Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding. In the past, including during Trump's first term as president, both Democrats and Republicans strongly supported foreign aid.

MORE SCRUTINY OF LATIN AMERICA POLICY

Trump has been far more aggressive in the western hemisphere than recent presidents, including the US military's ousting of Venezuela's president and more than a year of deadly strikes on boats off the country's coast.

He also has imposed sanctions seeking to hurt Cuba's communist government, with threats of military action to force a change in government. The US administration has also sought to influence elections in Honduras, Argentina, Colombia and Brazil.

Some Democrats have called for investigations and hearings on Trump's actions in Venezuela. Others have denounced what they term cruel sanctions punishing civilians in Cuba and called for an end to involvement in foreign elections.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle in Washington; Additional reporting by Richard Cowan in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: Mother of Ghanaian teen killed in New York heads to US funeral after Trump grants visa
items.content_html:
ACCRA, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The mother of a Ghanaian teenager who was fatally shot in New York departed for the United States on Wednesday after President Donald Trump intervened to grant her a visa to travel to attend her son's funeral.

  • Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old from Ghana, was fatally shot by unidentified assailants on October 29 in the Bronx, New York, while on his way to school, according to a statement on October 30 from Ghana's Foreign Ministry
  • Frimpong was living with his father after moving to the US from Ghana last year, the Associated Press has reported
  • Trump's intervention to grant the boy's mother, Doris Adu Gyamfi, a visa followed a phone call with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who requested his help to allow her to attend her son's funeral with relatives
  • "I want justice for my son. That's all," she told foreign affairs officials who accompanied her to the airport
  • Adu Gyamfi hoped that her son would study to become a doctor after moving to the US, she told them
  • Ghana called for a thorough investigation and urged New York authorities to bring those responsible for the killing to justice
  • New York police are investigating the killing, according to local media reports

Reporting by Emmanuel Bruce; Writing by Ayen Deng Bior; Editing by Jessica Donati and Xevi Fontdegloria

items.title: US services sector activity cools slightly in October; inflation remains elevated
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - US services sector growth slowed marginally in October amid a moderation in new orders, but supply chains remained strained, keeping prices for inputs elevated.

The Institute for Supply Management said on Wednesday its nonmanufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index dipped to 54.5 last month from 54.9 in September. A reading above 50 indicates growth in the services sector, which accounts for more than two-thirds of US economic activity. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI little changed at 54.8.

The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing, though economists expect a slowdown in activity, with consumer spending expected to pull back after back-to-back quarters of robust growth. Spending is seen in part curbed by high inflation, which is eroding household purchasing power.

Income at the disposal of households, after adjusting for inflation and taxes, fell in September after being unchanged in August. The saving rate is at a four-year low of 3.8%.

The survey's measure of new orders received by services businesses decreased to 55.9 last month from 59.8 in September. Delivery performance by suppliers deteriorated further against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and tariffs on imports. The Middle East conflict, now in its ninth month, has boosted energy prices and caused shortages of commodities that are shipped through the Strait of Hormuz.

The survey's measure of supplier deliveries jumped to 56.7 from 53.2 in September. A reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. Deliveries have slowed for 23 consecutive months, keeping input prices high.

The survey's measure of prices paid by businesses for inputs eased to a still-high 73.0 last month from 74.0 in September. The ISM on Monday reported a slight moderation in prices paid for inputs by manufacturers in October.

Economists expect inflation to continue to run above the Federal Reserve's 2% target into 2027. The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the US central bank to raise borrowing costs in December.

The ISM survey showed a marginal increase in services sector employment, aligning with economists' expectations for moderate growth in nonfarm payrolls in October. The survey's measure of services employment rose to 51.4 from 50.1 in September.

The government's closely watched employment report on Friday is likely to show payrolls advanced by 65,000 in October after increasing 29,000 in September, according to a Reuters survey of economists. The unemployment rate is forecast to have been unchanged at 4.2%.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate
items.content_html:
DETROIT, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's open US Senate seat on Tuesday, according to media projections, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber while preserving a crucial Democratic seat in the party's fight for Senate control.

El-Sayed's victory in the closely contested election marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Party's progressive wing and denied Republicans a chance to flip the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

El-Sayed, 42, a former public health official, focused on lowering costs for working families and reducing corporate influence in politics. His platform included Medicare for All, a government-funded universal healthcare program championed by progressives in his party.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday's midterm elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

His opponent Mike Rogers, 63, a former congressman and FBI agent, entered the race with strong backing from Trump and national Republicans and had sought to cast El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to Islamic extremism through alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims that El-Sayed denies and that remain unsupported by evidence. Democrats said the attacks on El-Sayed relied on Islamophobic tropes.

Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with El-Sayed's opposition to US military aid for Israel and his characterization of Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide.

But Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and Trump's low ratings. In the closing weeks of the race, he broke with the president on the war in Iran and the US trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.

Reporting by Nathan Layne; Editing by Howard Goller

items.title: US Democratic win unlikely to ease firms' cost, tariff woes in near term, executives say
items.content_html:
FRANKFURT/TOKYO/GDANSK, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global companies said on Wednesday that Democrats' capture of the United States Congress is unlikely to change their near-term outlook, as businesses struggle with higher costs of energy and raw materials and a stretched US consumer.

Some though welcomed the prospect of political stability.

Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

But it is too early to know what the results mean for the issues roiling companies worldwide, from tariffs and energy prices to inflation and consumer confidence.

Soaring costs related to the Iran war are the latest headache for companies making everything from food and drink to consumer electronics and cars, after contending last year with Trump's tariffs on imported goods.

High gas and grocery bills were big concerns among voters in the US midterm elections.

"What we need as a company in the US is political stability and a reliable economic framework. And everything which is embracing this is welcome," said Roland Welzbacher, CFO of German car parts supplier Continental (CONG.DE).

"What it really means for us and for the economy at large remains to be seen, but it brings stability, which is good."

Global stocks and the dollar rose after the results, although chip stocks in Asia came under pressure, as investors expect the Democratic-controlled Congress to apply more scrutiny to AI. GLOB/MKTS

The election outcome could also have broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.

WHITE HOUSE COULD FACE GREATER PRESSURE TO AVOID TRADE WARS

While analysts said the White House may face greater pressure to avoid a return to the trade wars that have raised costs for American consumers, some European manufacturers expect little immediate material relief from Trump's hefty import tariffs.

The administration largely pursued its tariff agenda through executive authorities that do not require congressional approval, and those powers remain in place, said Andrew Adair, trade policy adviser for North America at German machinery association VDMA.

Congress could seek to roll back existing tariffs, but such legislation would face major political hurdles and could ultimately be vetoed by the president, he said.

"We therefore do not anticipate national politics to directly impact business conditions over the short term," he told Reuters.

Kenichi Hori, president and chief executive of Japanese trading house Mitsui, which generates significant revenue in the United States, told media that he will be closely watching US policy on tariffs, critical minerals trade and AI data centre build-outs, but he expects the business environment to remain "highly uncertain".

RESULT COULD BOOST VISITOR NUMBERS

The result could improve the United States' image abroad, which has been hurt by Trump's tougher stance on immigration and trade policies, with visitor numbers dropping sharply since he took office.

"There might be less tariff-related irritation and a greater willingness to travel, which should have a rather positive impact on the aviation sector," Fraport CEO Stefan Schulte said. "But I wouldn't overestimate the significance of this."

Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management, was among those to warn of gridlock in Washington, saying that federal funding runs out on December 11 and that Trump has promised to become "Mr Veto" against a Democratic Congress.

"Divided government means gridlock, and gridlock means noise: investigations, vetoes, funding deadlines, and very likely another government shutdown or two, or more," he said.

items.title: 'A mandate for change': Democrats remake Texas politics in election rout
items.content_html:
Nov 4 (Reuters) - Texas Democrats, shut out of every statewide office for more than three decades, have toppled Republicans from the top of the ballot to the bottom, remaking the political landscape of the nation's largest conservative state in a single earth-shattering night.

While James Talarico's victory in the US Senate race and Gina Hinojosa's defeat of three-term Governor Greg Abbott stole the headlines, Democratic candidates also triumphed in a series of lower-profile races on Tuesday, giving them the power to reshape the state's economic and political future.

The Democratic wins were fueled by record turnout -- especially in Latino communities that have borne the brunt of President Donald Trump's immigration sweeps -- and cracks in the Republican coalition, as some conservatives and independents soured on inflation and the war with Iran.

“I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state,” Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “The voters have delivered a mandate for change and it is change they will get.”

Talarico, in a nod to the hundreds of millions of dollars that Elon Musk poured into his opponent's campaign, told his supporters “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”

Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, who as head of the state Senate has driven Texas' hard-right legislative agenda for more than a decade, lost to Vikki Goodwin, a state representative little known outside of the capital Austin.

Democrat Nathan Johnson captured the attorney general's office -- which Republicans have used for decades to challenge the policies of Democratic presidents in court.

Democrats also won races for comptroller, land commissioner, agriculture commissioner and railroad commissioner -- key offices that oversee the state budget, its public lands, its farm economy and its oil and gas industry.

As was true elsewhere in the US, efforts by Texas Republicans to redraw congressional maps to their advantage largely backfired on Tuesday. Tejano singer Bobby Pulido ousted Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz in the Rio Grande Valley; Democrat Katy Padilla Stout won the sprawling 23rd district.

A 'WAKE-UP CALL'

The last open question on Wednesday was whether Democrats would also take the Texas House, which Republicans have controlled since 2003.

Erika Kinder, a Republican voter attending the watch party for losing Senate candidate Ken Paxton, said she hoped the losses would re-energize her party.

“The Texas GOP has been a little softer and unenthusiastic and this is probably a good wake-up call,” she said. “I think we'll be right as rain in two to four years.”

Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democrats, predicted in a September interview with Reuters that the party would win at the top of the ticket -- and “we're going to surprise you down ballot, too.”

Scudder emerged from the party's grassroots and tried to steer it back to its populist roots. Talarico, Hinojosa and others on the Democratic ticket focused intensely on pocketbook issues and government corruption, even as their Republican opponents tried to center transgender rights and other culture war issues.

“This has been two years of everyone in this state trying to build in regions that have been ignored for a very long time, and in communities that have been taken for granted,” Scudder said weeks before the election. “It's going to culminate in wins.”

items.title: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
items.content_html:
HONG KONG/LONDON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Data center opponents were among the biggest winners of the Democrats' landslide victories in the US midterm elections, pointing to a shifting public mood on AI and, investors said, a possible slowdown of the boom that has propelled US economic growth and stock markets.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus on Wednesday. But in gubernatorial races in Texas and Georgia, Democrats who campaigned in part on a moratorium on data center development won offices that the party has not held for decades.

Their victories hand political heft to opponents of the projects, which are at the heart of the AI boom but are loud, thirsty for water, hungry for electricity and increasingly unpopular with their neighbours, investors said.

US-based data center stocks slid as the Democratic sweep became apparent. Core Scientific (CORZ.O) fell 11.6% and Iren (IREN.O) tumbled 12.5%, while other AI infrastructure firms such as Applied Digital (APLD.O), Hut 8 Corp (HUT.O), Cipher Digital (CIFR.O) and power firms such as GE Vernova (GEV.N), Constellation Energy (CEG.O) and Vistra (VST.N) slumped.

Investors said the results are likely to usher in tougher regulation and could ripple across financial markets where AI stocks were falling on Wednesday; big bets have already started to wobble due to concerns about spending and overcapacity.

"In our view, the significance of these midterm elections is more like a referendum on AI than a referendum on (Donald) Trump," said Aidan Yao, a senior investment strategist at the Amundi Investment Institute, the research arm of Europe's largest asset manager.

"If the AI theme is subject to some restrictions, then the US economy, US inflation and US monetary policy all become very, very uncertain."

In the mix too is the upcoming IPO of Anthropic, which is preparing to begin formally marketing shares to prospective investors next week. An amended regulatory filing on Monday showed Anthropic's net loss narrowed in the third quarter, as revenue surged 47% from a quarter earlier to $16.96 billion, though the pace of growth slowed.

TEXAS SWEEP

The most stunning ballot box repudiation was in Texas, which GLJ Research has estimated accounts for about a quarter of US data center capacity due to come online by 2030.

But Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott as governor in an upset that ended three decades of Republican hold on the office, while fellow party member James Talarico became the senator-elect.

A conservative, oil-producing state, Texas has worked for years to reinvent itself as a tech hub, attracting companies such as SpaceX (SPCX.O) and entrepreneurs like Elon Musk, who donated more than $150 million to Ken Paxton, the Republican who lost to Talarico.

But even Republicans turned against data centers, which opponents say drive up utility bills, pollute the night sky with lights and do not create sufficient jobs or taxes to justify the incentives that states pay.

"Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said on social media after the election.

Goldman Sachs said Democratic victories at the state and local level would likely lead to temporary halts to projects, potentially affecting some 45% of planned US data centre capacity expansion, though they think it will be short-lived.

In Georgia, where commercial real estate services and investment firm CBRE says Atlanta is the most active data center construction market in the country, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial contest, ending more than two decades of Republican control.

How widely the data center and AI business is affected remains to be seen, HSBC analysts Max Kettner and Duncan Toms wrote.

"One possible – and entirely feasible – scenario is that we won't see broad-based data center moratoriums but rather more regulations/higher oversight on data centers," they said. "Another one is that data centers simply move from Texas to other states."

Analysts at Morgan Stanley said the election of Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio as governor creates a significant risk of data center project delays in that state, including a 10-gigawatt project involving Nvidia (NVDA.O) that is the largest in the state. Ohio put a moratorium earlier this year on considering new data center tax exemption requests.

THE AI TRADE

AI growth has driven stocks higher this year due to bets on chip demand while pushing up bond yields, as the data center construction boom boosts economic growth.

Chip and AI firms like TSMC (2330.TW), Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Kioxia (285A.T) fell in Asia – along with bond yields – on Wednesday.

To be sure, many analysts said a slowdown in the building of data centers in the US did not necessarily herald a change in demand for AI or computing power, and some view a roughly 8% drawdown in the Nasdaq (.IXIC) over the past month as an opportunity to buy.

Tommaso Leodari, Dubai-based chief investment officer of hedge fund Index & Cie, said the risks for data centers were difficult to predict, given their vital role in America's competition with China.

"I do not foresee limitations, higher taxes, or other kinds of opposition to the force behind a new industrial revolution for the US. I consider that Dems are going to continue being more moderate than before, so any fury will be directed at Trump and his team, not at a new industry that can save American imperialism," he said.

Reporting by Jiaxing Li and Selena Li; Writing by Tom Westbrook; Additional reporting by Tom Westbrook, Amanda Cooper, Sruthi Shankar, Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus and David Gaffen

items.title: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot in the midterm elections and handpicked Republican candidates in some of the country's most consequential Senate races. By Tuesday night, voters had rejected them.

Trump-backed candidates in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas and Michigan all lost, handing Democrats control of the chamber and exposing the limits of Trump's political power.

Trump has spent more than a decade reshaping the Republican Party around his MAGA movement, dictating primary matchups and pushing aside conservative figures he felt were insufficiently loyal or not aligned with his vision. Trump repeatedly favored loyalists and ideological allies over more established Republicans with stronger statewide networks and proven electoral track records, betting that his endorsement could overcome their political liabilities.

Tuesday's results revealed he was unable to persuade the broader electorate to back his choices.

One of the most stunning repudiations came in South Carolina, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998 and which Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024. Trump backed Darline Graham, the sister of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham. But Democrat Annie Andrews won the seat in a stunning upset.

In North Carolina, Trump endorsed former national Republican campaign official Michael Whatley, who lost in a rout to former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

In Texas, Trump intervened in a messy Republican primary election to promote scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn, a Trump ally who some in the party considered a safer pick in the general election. Democrat James Talarico glided to a victory on Tuesday night, delivering Democrats a seat the party had not won since 1988.

Former US Representative Mike Rogers, Trump's choice in Michigan, was defeated by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who will be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate.

The losses came as Trump's popularity was lower heading into Tuesday's vote than in the aftermath of the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol, according to Reuters/Ipsos polls. That helped fuel concerns among Republicans that the president had become a drag on the party he remade around himself.

"This is a Trump Quake," said Doug Heye, a veteran Republican strategist, pointing to voter frustration over high prices caused by tariffs and the war in Iran. "Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not to them."

Trump struck a defiant tone as election returns arrived.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote in a Tuesday night social media post.

One White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump "did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves."

A senior White House official, also speaking anonymously, told Reuters the administration had polling data as far back as six weeks ago showing Republicans would lose both the House of Representatives and Senate, and Trump embarked on a month-long nationwide campaign to try to salvage Republicans' prospects.

'GAVE THAT SEAT AWAY'

Some independent analysts said the Senate losses bore Trump's fingerprints specifically. Thomas Kahn, a professor at American University, said the president's intervention in the Texas Republican primary had cost his party a safe seat, arguing that a nomination for Senator John Cornyn "would have been a slam dunk for Republicans to win."

North Carolina, Kahn said, was another clear case. The Republican incumbent senator, Thom Tillis, said he would not seek re-election last year after a public split with Trump, who threatened to back a primary challenger against him after Tillis balked at Medicaid cuts in the president's tax-and-spending bill.

"He essentially gave that seat away to Democrats," Kahn said. "Roy Cooper would not have run if Thom Tillis had run for re-election."

Former North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory, a Republican, said Trump's interventions in his party's primaries had divided Republicans in state after state.

In South Carolina, McCrory said, the president went against two local congressmen, a fight that "really divided the party" — an example, in his telling, of a president spending his political capital against his own side.

McCrory's sharpest criticism was aimed at Trump's connection with the voters who built his coalition.

"I think President Trump's greatest strength was he had a common touch with the working class people," McCrory said. "He lost that skill. He better regain that skill for the good of the country."

items.title: Prediction markets get Democratic win right, with a few surprises
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Prediction markets largely got the big picture right in the US midterm elections but underestimated the strength of many Democratic candidates, who delivered a string of surprises as they seized control of the Senate and House of Representatives, preliminary results and private analyses showed Wednesday.

With billions wagered on Tuesday's elections, the results offered a test of whether prediction markets could translate their odds into accurate electoral forecasts.

Bets placed on a Democratic midterm sweep largely paid off despite some mispriced races, as tens of millions of voters delivered a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump.

"Prediction markets priced the midterm outcome within hours," said Kelly Ye, head of research at digital asset trading platform Talos.

Several closely contested Senate races had attracted millions of dollars in bets, putting prediction markets under scrutiny. In many cases, the results tracked expectations, with Democrats winning Senate seats in Texas and Ohio.

"This was the first true prediction markets election," said Harry Crane, professor of statistics at Rutgers University.

"The markets projected Democratic wins across the board throughout the closing weeks of the campaign, and were quick to react in real time to voting information as it rolled in," he added.

Prediction markets rose to prominence as they diverged from traditional opinion polls by signaling a Trump victory in 2024, and analysts were scrutinizing their performance this week.

According to prediction market Kalshi, traders led the way in predicting that Democrats would take control of the Senate in this year's elections, forecasting this outcome as early as April. Kalshi's own assessments of its accuracy showed that on the whole it was more accurate than other leading forecasting models, according to statistics the company released Wednesday morning. Reuters could not independently verify the data the company released.

However, both prediction markets and polls appeared to face difficulty on Tuesday night in forecasting some of the same races: In the first prediction market upset of the night, Democrat Annie Andrews of South Carolina bested Republican Darline Graham, who had been favored to win with market odds of about 70%.

Likewise, Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa defied similar odds to unseat the state's incumbent Governor Greg Abbott. Meanwhile, as of Wednesday's vote tallying, Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom was a hair's breadth ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, whom markets on election day had heavily favored to win.

Analytics firm BETINT also said that, out of more than 400 races for which results are known so far, all known upset victories had gone to Democrats, with 14 of them defeating opponents who the week before had been the odds-on favorites to win.

This showed Democrats had repeatedly outperformed the probabilities assigned to them by prediction markets, it said in an election research bulletin, which also concluded that prediction markets and polls had performed about equally well overall in picking winners.

Those upsets also followed the high-profile market miss last month in Brazil's presidential election.

Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to real-world events, with prices reflecting traders' collective expectations. Critics, however, say those odds can be skewed by speculation, thin liquidity and concentrated bets.

Kalshi's total trading volume on election markets reached over $2.5 billion this cycle, compared with $1.3 billion during the 2024 election cycle, which included the presidential race.

Traders on Kalshi were assigning a 55% probability to a "blue tsunami" as early as April. Meanwhile, Polymarket's election forecasts were about 98% accurate, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Polymarket said its traders had wagered nearly $700 million during this election cycle across both its US and international platforms.

"Prediction markets can be useful because they aggregate the views of people who have an incentive to be right, not just to express an opinion," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.

"They can give a good indication of where the weight of information is pointing, but a prediction isn't a promise. Whether it's politics or sports, you still have to hold the election or play the game to know the result," he added.

Reporting by Douglas Gillison and Michelle Price in Washington and Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Michelle Price, Deepa Babington, Lincoln Feast, Alexander Smith and Aurora Ellis

items.title: Explainer: What's next for Alaska's unusual US Senate race
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The outcome of the US Senate race in Alaska was unclear on Wednesday, one day after Democrats scored a sweeping victory in the US midterm elections that delivered them control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. With an unusual voting system and a legal challenge by the Trump administration, it could be weeks until a result is known.

Here's what we know — and what we don't — about the Last Frontier's Senate race.

WHO ARE THE CANDIDATES AND WHAT ARE THE RESULTS SO FAR?

Incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, first elected in 2014, is locked in a tight battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, a centrist who served one term in the US House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025. Alaska is typically a reliably Republican state — President Donald Trump won it by 13 points in 2024 — but also displays an independent streak. The state's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, won re-election as a write-in candidate in 2010 after she lost the Republican primary.

Two other candidates were also on the general-election ballot: retired schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan, who has no party affiliation, and Republican Gerry Heikes, a drywall contractor.

With ballots still being counted, Peltola led Senator Sullivan by fewer than 700 votes, 48.2% to 47.9%, while retired teacher Sullivan has so far won about 3,600 votes, or 1.7%, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today, which are partnering this year to collect live election results. Heikes has so far won 2.3% of the vote, or fewer than 5,000 ballots.

WHY DON'T WE KNOW THE RESULTS YET?

Alaska runs a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can rank candidates on their ballots in order of preference rather than selecting only one. The top four vote-getters in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.

To win the general election, candidates need to receive more than 50% of the vote. If no candidate receives more than half of voters' first-place votes, officials eliminate the last-place finisher and reallocate those ballots to voters' next choices until one candidate has a majority.

Because it takes time for officials to count every ballot in the first round of voting, it could be weeks until a winner is declared. Officials will not run the ranked-choice tabulation until November 18.

THE DOUBLE DAN CONTROVERSY

Republicans had long alleged that Dan J. Sullivan was a spoiler candidate, meant to confuse voters who wanted to vote for the incumbent senator and did not know the difference between the two Sullivans.

Republicans tried to remove Sullivan the teacher from the ballot, alleging he was not a "good faith" candidate. But Alaska's highest court rebuffed that argument.

The New York Times reported last week that Peltola's campaign helped recruit Dan J. Sullivan into the race. Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement.

The Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations, a probe it widened this week. Department officials have sent letters to more than 20 people notifying them they are subjects of the criminal probe, according to two people familiar with the investigation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss it.

Those are among the more than 140 letters, subpoenas and notices that have been sent in the probe, including to Democrats, campaigns, political action committees and phone companies, one of the people said.

Targets include prominent voting rights lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm has represented Democrats including Peltola, according to the people. Trump said on Tuesday Elias should be in jail. Elias has denied any wrongdoing.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

The Justice Department's letters do not serve as evidence of guilt, and department officials have struggled to successfully bring convictions against many of Trump's perceived enemies.

If Peltola does win, Republicans could also seek to appeal her victory and block her from being seated — but they will have less leverage with Democrats in control of the Senate from January.

The Justice Department has given no indication that it will ease up. On Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche sought to cast doubt on the ranked-choice voting system and called for Alaska to preserve the ballots cast in the state.

"The Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process," Blanche said. "We're not going to stop the fight even after today."

items.title: Democrat Troy Jackson ousts Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins conceded to Democrat Troy Jackson on Tuesday, scoring a major pickup for Democrats in one of the midterms' most competitive races.

First elected in 1996, Collins had repeatedly survived as a moderate Republican in a state that has not backed her party for president since 1988. But this year she faced economic headwinds that helped Jackson overcome his late entry into the race.

The Iran war pushed up fuel and home heating oil prices – an especially salient issue in a largely rural state known for harsh winters. Trump's trade war with Canada weighed on tourism, lobstering, logging and other pillars of Maine's economy.

Jackson, a former state Senate president, emphasized his blue-collar roots as a fifth-generation logger from the remote town of Allagash. He campaigned on universal healthcare and other populist policies, drawing the support of high-profile progressives like Senator Bernie Sanders, a democratic socialist from Vermont.

Jackson, 58, took an unusual path to victory. He initially campaigned for governor, but came in third place in the crowded Democratic primary in June. Democrats selected him as their Senate nominee in July to replace Graham Platner, a former Marine and oysterman who dropped out after facing rape allegations, which he denied.

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the midterm elections to take back control of the chamber.

Reporting by Andy Sullivan; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Howard Goller

items.title: Trump acknowledges role of Iran war in Democratic sweep in midterm elections
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the US-Israeli war on Iran played a role in his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

"I think a part of it was Iran," Trump told Fox News in an interview; "Iran was a piece of it," he separately told The Wall Street Journal.

But despite the Republican losses on Tuesday -- and his campaign promise of "no new wars" -- Trump stood by his decision to attack Iran.

"I did the right thing," he said in his interview with the Wall Street Journal. "I would have done it again."

The war, now in its ninth month, has been unpopular among Americans since it began. On the campaign trail, Democratic candidates across the country blamed the conflict for driving up the cost of gas and other goods.

Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war, alternately threatening to ramp up US military strikes and saying he could end the conflict at any time.

In Tehran, the US election results were met with satisfaction. "Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Wednesday on X.

Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Jarrett Renshaw; Editing by Christian Schmollinger, Howard Goller and Alistair Bell

items.title: Democrat Rob Sand wins Iowa governor race, projections show
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand defeated Republican businessman Zach Lahn to become the first Democratic governor elected in the state since 2006, according to US media projections.

He will replace outgoing Governor Kim Reynolds.

Sand campaigned as an independent-minded Democrat who sought to appeal to voters from all parties. He was known to ask rally attendees to sing “America the Beautiful.”

Like other Iowa candidates, he campaigned heavily on addressing the state’s rising incidence of cancer, the second highest in the nation after Kentucky.

He distanced himself from progressive positions on transgender issues, taking a similar approach to other moderate Midwest Democratic candidates hoping to win rural voters.

Reporting by Ryan Patrick Jones; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Deepa Babington

items.title: Adam Hamilton becomes first Democrat elected to US Senate from Kansas in 94 years
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - Adam Hamilton won the US Senate race in Kansas on Tuesday, according to media projections, ousting Trump-backed Republican Roger Marshall to become the state's first Democrat elected senator in 94 years and helping Democrats cement control of the chamber.

It was a striking Democratic gain in a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and where the race had initially been expected to be safely Republican.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday's elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

Hamilton, pastor of the country's largest United Methodist congregation, campaigned on affordability and bipartisanship, calling himself an "independent-minded Democrat" and rejecting Republican portrayals of him as far left.

Wearing a pin that said "love one another," Hamilton spoke in his victory speech of the need for unity between Democrats and Republicans, and for curbing cost of living increases caused by Trump policies like tariffs and cuts to food assistance.

In electing him, "the people in Kansas, Republicans, Democrats and independents, were saying, what's happening in Washington is not okay," Hamilton said.

The race tightened in its final weeks, drawing Trump and Vice President JD Vance to Kansas to campaign for Marshall.

At a Wichita-area campaign rally on October 19, Trump said the US Department of Agriculture would launch a "harvest fuel relief program" to provide farmers with $8 billion to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

Hamilton, 62, has written more than 30 books on Christianity and theology.

He and Marshall both sought to appeal to Kansas farmers hit by high diesel and fertilizer prices driven up in part by the war in Iran.

Marshall, an obstetrician before entering politics, was elected to the US House in 2016 and the Senate in 2020. He faced criticism after a New York Times report in September said he had sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. In a September interview with Fox News, he called the article a "hit job" and said he followed typical collections practices.

Reporting by Leah Douglas in Washington; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Howard Goller and Daniel Wallis

attachments.title: Democratic candidate for US Senate from Kansas Adam Hamilton reacts to election results in his hotel suite at a Marriott hotel in Overland Park, Kansas, US, November 3, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

items.title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats Texas Governor Abbott in a stunning upset
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Rtrs) - Three-term Republican Texas Governor Greg Abbott lost to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa in a stunning upset that ends the Republican Party's three-decade hold on the governor's office, US media projected on Tuesday.

Hinojosa makes history as the first Hispanic elected to lead the state. No Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, the longest drought in the nation. It was another surprising result during a strong night for Democrats, who were projected to win control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate with victories in conservative states such as South Carolina and Kansas.

Hinojosa's strategy hinged in part on persuading Latino voters that rising costs and strained public schools matter more than the cultural war issues that have pulled many Latino voters toward Republicans in recent years.

"We are as Texan and American as anyone," she said in a July interview with Reuters in Austin. "Latinos are feeling the economic strain just like families all across this country and in Texas in a big way."

Abbott spent years cultivating support in South Texas, regularly visiting heavily Latino border communities, building an extensive field operation in the Rio Grande Valley and making border security a centerpiece of his outreach.

Hinojosa emerged as an unexpected competitor to one of the best-known and best-funded Republican governors in the country.

Her win comes alongside that of State Representative James Talarico's victory in the US Senate race in Texas, according to media projections. He defeated President Donald Trump-backed Republican candidate Ken Paxton.

The Democratic wins were a result of Latinos turning out to vote, motivated by affordability concerns and Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement agenda, according to Voto Latino Executive Director Beatriz Lopez.

The organization, which works to register and mobilize Latino voters, registered about 400,000 voters in Texas this election cycle and hopes to carry the momentum into the 2028 presidential election.

"This is a Texas sweep," she said. "It has literally put Texas on the map as a battleground state - and that changes everything now and into 2028."

Hinojosa's win is part of a broader Democratic rout in Republican bastions as voters rejected Trump, his handling of the economy and the war with Iran.

items.title: Democrat Sherrod Brown wins back US Senate seat in Ohio
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Sherrod Brown won Ohio's special US Senate election on Tuesday, according to US media projections, ousting Republican incumbent Jon Husted and boosting his party's chances of winning a majority in the chamber.

Brown's victory marked a comeback two years after losing his Senate seat and showed that Democrats could still win statewide in Ohio, where Republicans have become dominant since Trump's political rise in 2016.

His 2024 loss to Republican Senator Bernie Moreno ended Brown's 18-year tenure in the Senate.

Husted was appointed to the Senate by Republican Governor Mike DeWine in January 2025 to replace JD Vance after he became vice president. The special election was to determine who serves the remainder of Vance's term, through January 3, 2029.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. In Tuesday's nationwide midterm elections, Democrats must score a net gain of four seats to win control of the chamber beginning in January.

President Donald Trump endorsed Husted and campaigned with him in the closing weeks of the campaign. At a time when 78% of Americans blame Trump for the high cost of living, the president campaigned in Ohio to help energize Republicans' base of voters who otherwise might have sat out the election.

Former President Barack Obama appeared in campaign ads for Brown.

Reporting by Richard Cowan; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Howard Goller

attachments.title: Democratic US Senate candidate Sherrod Brown takes the stage at a Democratic Election Night rally during the US midterm elections, in Columbus, Ohio, US, November 3, 2026. REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton

items.title: US moves to drop frog embryo smuggling charges against Harvard scientist
items.content_html:
BOSTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - US prosecutors moved on Tuesday to drop criminal charges against a Russian-born scientist at Harvard University accused of smuggling frog embryos into the United States after she argued the Trump administration had singled her out for prosecution.

Federal prosecutors in Boston said in a court filing they were dismissing the charges against Kseniia Petrova after a federal judge cleared the way for her to obtain evidence supporting her claim that she was being vindictively prosecuted.

Prosecutors in the filing said that while they viewed those claims as "meritless," continuing to prosecute the case after the judge's order "would divert significant time and attention from more substantial federal interests."

"Throughout these proceedings, Ms. Petrova has shown tremendous courage, and we are relieved that this chapter of her terrible ordeal will soon be over," William Fick, her lawyer, said in a statement.

A spokesperson for US Attorney Leah Foley, the Trump administration's top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts, declined to comment.

The biomedical researcher had been taken into custody by US immigration authorities at the airport in Boston in February 2025 after her visa was revoked upon her return from a trip to France.

Prosecutors brought a criminal case against Petrova, who worked at Harvard Medical School, in May 2025 as a federal judge in Vermont weighed ordering her release from the immigration detention facility in Louisiana.

Prosecutors alleged that US Customs and Border Protection agents stopped Petrova after her checked duffel bag was flagged for inspection, revealing the frog embryos that they said should have been declared to customs officials.

Petrova, who was ultimately released on bail in June 2025, pleaded not guilty to the smuggling and false statement charges she faced. She has said her boss asked her to bring back frog embryo samples for experiments.

Her lawyers argued the charges were brought in retaliation for her decision to challenge the immigration proceedings against her and said that the case had been brought amid a broader campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against researchers, universities and Harvard itself.

In April, a federal judge in Vermont ruled Petrova's visa had been unlawfully canceled. And last month, a judge in Boston sustained a decision that concluded she put forward sufficient evidence that she was selectively prosecuted to entitle her to obtain access to government records to support her claim.

Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Stephen Coates

items.title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win statewide in Texas since 1994
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - State Representative James Talarico won the US Senate race in Texas on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton to end Democrats' 32-year statewide losing streak and give his party a major boost in the battle for Senate control.

It was a striking Democratic breakthrough in a state Republicans have long dominated. Trump carried the state by 14 percentage points in 2024. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, has been at the center of controversies that include a 2023 impeachment and a securities fraud case.

Talarico, a four-term state legislator and one of the nation's top Senate fundraisers, overcame heavy outside spending in the most expensive Senate race of the cycle. He began as an underdog against former US Representative Colin Allred, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee, who later withdrew to run for Congress again.

Talarico went on to defeat US Representative Jasmine Crockett for the Democratic nomination, dealing a political blow to his former state legislative colleague.

Republicans spent more than $316 million to retain the seat. Republican US Senator John Cornyn was ousted in a primary runoff after Trump endorsed Paxton. Republican leaders had viewed Cornyn as the stronger general-election candidate.

Paxton used his role as attorney general to sue former President Joe Biden's administration more than 100 times.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday's elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Howard Goller

items.title: Trump says he is willing to accept midterm election results, NYT reports
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said in an interview with the New York Times on Tuesday that he was willing to accept the results of the midterm elections in which his Republican Party was projected to lose control of the US House.

"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," Trump was quoted as saying by the Times.

items.title: Democrat Acton defeats Republican Ramaswamy in Ohio governor race
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Rtrs) - Democratic candidate Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the race to become Ohio's next governor, a seat currently held by a Republican, US media projected on Tuesday.

Reporting by Michelle Nichols; Editing by Caitlin Webber

items.title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins US Senate seat in South Carolina upset
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Annie Andrews won a US Senate seat in conservative South Carolina on Tuesday, according to media projections, ousting Republican Darline Graham in a state President Donald Trump carried by 18 percentage points just two years ago.

Andrews, a pediatrician, is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in South Carolina in 28 years, a striking gain for a party that needed a net four seats to overturn Republicans' 53-47 majority.

Andrews' win in a state that neither Democrats nor Republicans considered competitive until recent weeks embodies the broader rejection of Trump and his handling of the economy during the first two years of his term.

The South Carolina Senate race attracted national attention after Darline Graham's brother, US Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly in July. Trump lobbied Governor Henry McMaster to appoint his sister — a little-known state employee who had never held elected office — to fill the late senator's seat and publicly encouraged her to run for the full term.

She defeated US Representative Ralph Norman for the Republican nomination in an August runoff, but divisions lingered. Norman told local media that he would vote for her but his family would not, and he declined to campaign with her.

Graham's inexperience was on display during a Republican runoff debate in August, when she said she was not "that informed on national security" and that national security was "not my thing." Senate Majority Leader John Thune did not endorse Graham but said she was a strong candidate. Former Republican Governor David Beasley and former Democratic Governor Jim Hodges jointly endorsed Andrews.

Republicans had privately worried that Graham was a weak candidate, according to a party strategist who spoke on condition of anonymity, and grew increasingly frustrated when the national party had to divert resources to prop her up. Republican outside groups poured $27 million into holding the seat, while Democratic groups invested $24 million to flip it.

Graham has said she was "not a polished politician" but defended her candidacy, saying during an October debate against Andrews that she was "just as qualified" as her opponent.

DEMOCRATS NOTCH OTHER SURPRISE WINS

Trump's approval rating has held near a career low amid voter discontent with the Iran war, high diesel prices and the cost of living, putting once solidly Republican seats into play.

Trump held a rally in the state last week as the race tightened, where Graham told supporters her opponent was "batshit crazy." In response, Andrews asked Graham if it was crazy "to want cheaper gas and groceries."

Democrats notched surprise wins in other closely watched House and Senate races in their drive to retake control of both chambers of Congress. The party has vowed to launch aggressive investigations of Trump officials and cabinet members, as well as companies that made concessions to the White House or capitulated to Trump's demands.

In addition to South Carolina, Democrats picked up Senate seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Texas, according to media projections.

"This night is turning into a very clear repudiation of Trump, MAGA and the Republican party," said Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic strategist.

Republicans held onto Florida's Senate seat in a tighter-than-expected race, as Republican Ashley Moody edged past Democrat Angie Nixon.

Democrats also defended several House seats in redrawn districts meant to favor Republicans in North Carolina, Florida and other states, and were on track to win House seats in what had been considered safe Republican districts in deeply conservative states.

Reporting by Yasmeen Abutaleb; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Howard Goller and Edmund Klamann
